verdict.summary:
QUALIFICATIONS FOR INSPECTION AUTHORIZATION (IA) WITH RESPECT TO MAJOR ALTERATIONS
14 CFR (eCFR) - FAA-AMT context - Regulatory analysis

====================================================================
0. SCOPE AND INTERPRETATION (stated, not assumed silently)
====================================================================
- 'Inspection auth' is read as the Inspection Authorization issued under 14 CFR Part 65, Subpart D - not the general return-to-service authority of a certificated mechanic.
- 'Major alteration' is read in the regulatory sense of 14 CFR 1.1 and Part 43 Appendix A.
- Subject aircraft: U.S.-registered civil aircraft in standard/restricted category. The 65.95(a)(1) carve-out for aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program is noted.
- OUT OF SCOPE (not asked, and not determinable from the sources without the aircraft model and the alteration data): whether a specific alteration must be approved by STC versus FAA field approval. That determination drives which data package the IA inspects against, but it does not change the IA qualification requirements, which are the subject of this answer.
- Source currency: eCFR text captured 2026-11-13T22:57:02Z (source hashes recorded in the research set). Re-verify before use in a certification or enforcement-sensitive document.

====================================================================
1. ONE-LINE ANSWER
====================================================================
The qualification that matters for inspecting and approving a major alteration for return to service is the Inspection Authorization under 14 CFR Part 65, Subpart D. To hold it, the applicant must (i) hold a current mechanic certificate with BOTH airframe and powerplant ratings, each in effect for a total of at least 3 years, (ii) have a fixed base of operations, (iii) be actively engaged in the maintenance and alteration of aircraft, (iv) have the equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, and related parts/appliances, and (v) pass the IA written test - which by regulation is a test on the applicant's ability to inspect 'according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations and annual and progressive inspections performed under part 43.' The privilege itself is conferred by 14 CFR 65.95(a)(1), and it is conditioned on the alteration having been done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator.

====================================================================
2. THE OPERATIVE RULE CHAIN (in order)
====================================================================
Step 1 - Is it a major alteration? 14 CFR 1.1 defines 'major alteration' as an alteration not listed in the aircraft, aircraft engine, or propeller specifications that (1) might appreciably affect weight, balance, structural strength, performance, powerplant operation, flight characteristics, or other qualities affecting airworthiness, or (2) is not done according to accepted practices or cannot be done by elementary operations. Part 43 Appendix A lists specific operations that are major alterations (airframe, powerplant, propeller, appliance). The classification is the trigger for everything below.

Step 2 - Approval for return to service. 14 CFR 43.5(a) bars any person from approving for return to service an aircraft, airframe, engine, propeller, or appliance that has undergone maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, or alteration unless the 43.9/43.11 record entry has been made, the Administrator's repair/alteration form has been executed, and any resulting change to operating limitations or approved flight manual data has been incorporated.

Step 3 - Who is authorized. 14 CFR 43.7(b) provides that the holder of a mechanic certificate or an inspection authorization may approve for return to service as provided in Part 65. The same section lists the other authorized categories (the Administrator; repair stations under Part 145; manufacturers; air carriers/operators).

Step 4 - The IA privilege, 14 CFR 65.95(a)(1), quoted verbatim from the fetched eCFR page:

  'The holder of an inspection authorization may-
   (1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 [New] of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; and
   (2) Perform an annual, or perform or supervise a progressive inspection according to 43.13 and 43.15 of this chapter.'

  Two conditions are embedded in that privilege and are the crux of the AMT exam answer:
  (a) the work must have been done in accordance with technical data APPROVED by the Administrator (not merely 'acceptable' data); and
  (b) the aircraft must not be one maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program.

Step 5 - The approval data. Because 65.95(a)(1) keys to approved technical data, the IA's inspection is an inspection against an approved data package (STC, amended TC, or FAA field-approved data). FAA AC 43-210A states: 'The use of technical data approved by the Administrator for major alterations or major repairs to type certificated (TC) products is required by the following 14 CFR parts: Part 43, sections 43.7(d) and 43.17(e)(2); Part 65, section 65.95(a)(1) ... amended TC or STC.' (Quoted as captured; the paragraph letters as printed in the AC should be confirmed against current eCFR text before relying on the paragraph-level cites - the operative rule relied on here is 65.95(a)(1) and 43.7(b).) FAA field-approval guidance also states that alterations exceeding the basic scope of a field approval 'must be processed as an STC.'

====================================================================
3. IA ELIGIBILITY - 14 CFR 65.91 (the 'qualifications')
====================================================================
Elements, in substance:
  1. Application on the form and in the manner prescribed by the Administrator (65.91(a)).
  2. Current, effective mechanic certificate with BOTH an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each currently effective and in effect for a total of at least 3 years.
  3. A fixed base of operations at which the holder can be located/contacted.
  4. Actively engaged in the maintenance and alteration of aircraft.
  5. Available equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, and related parts or appliances.
  6. Pass the IA written test. Verbatim from the fetched eCFR page: 'Pass a written test on his ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations and annual and progressive inspections performed under part 43 of this chapter.'

Note on item 2: the 3-year figure applies to the mechanic certificate with both ratings; there is no separately stated numeric 'recent activity' threshold in 65.91 beyond the 'actively engaged' element (item 4). Do not restate a '2 of the last 3 years' figure for IA eligibility - that is not in the text I can source.

Duration and renewal:
  - 65.92: each inspection authorization expires on March 31 of each odd-numbered year (a 2-year cycle).
  - 65.93: renewal requires the holder to show qualifying activity during the 12 months before expiration - activity is measured per 90-day period (annual inspections performed; major repairs or major alterations performed; progressive inspections performed or supervised) - or completion of an acceptable refresher/renewal course. Confirm the exact option list and paragraph letters against the current eCFR text before quoting.

====================================================================
4. WHAT THE IA MAY AND MAY NOT DO ON A MAJOR ALTERATION
====================================================================
MAY: inspect and approve for return to service an aircraft or related part/appliance after a major alteration, where the work was done per Administrator-approved technical data, on aircraft not maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program (65.95(a)(1)).
MAY: perform annual and perform/supervise progressive inspections (65.95(a)(2)).
MAY NOT: approve for return to service a major alteration that was not accomplished in accordance with approved technical data. There is no IA discretion to 'bless' an alteration done on unapproved data; that is the boundary the regulation draws and it is the most commonly tested limitation.
MAY NOT (by the express carve-out): act under 65.95(a)(1) on aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program.

====================================================================
5. WHO ELSE MAY APPROVE A MAJOR ALTERATION FOR RETURN TO SERVICE
====================================================================
14 CFR 43.7 lists the authorized categories: the Administrator (which includes an FAA airworthiness inspector signing a field approval); the holder of a mechanic certificate or inspection authorization (as provided in Part 65); the holder of a repair station certificate (Part 145); a manufacturer for work it performed; and air carrier/operator certificate holders. Practical consequence for the AMT: on a major alteration, the signature on FAA Form 337, block 3 (Approval for Return to Service), is normally an IA or an FAA inspector - not a basic A&P acting alone.

Conservative compliance position for a mechanic WITHOUT an IA: do not sign off a major alteration for return to service absent (a) written confirmation from the certificate-holding district office/FSDO, or (b) an approved data package whose installation instructions expressly convey that return-to-service authority. The safe, teachable rule for FAA-AMT purposes is: minor alteration - mechanic may approve; major alteration - IA (or repair station / FAA field approval) approves.

====================================================================
6. RECORDS AND PAPERWORK THE IA'S APPROVAL TRIGGERS
====================================================================
- 43.9: maintenance/alteration record entry - description of work, date of completion, name, signature, certificate number, and the approval-for-return-to-service statement.
- 43.5(a): approval is not valid until the record entry and the Administrator's repair/alteration form are executed, and any operating-limitation or flight-manual change is incorporated.
- FAA Form 337, Major Repair and Alteration: the block-3 return-to-service approval; submission to the FAA per the form's instructions and FAA Order 8900.1 (Vol. 4, Ch. 9) - confirm current submission timing in the Order rather than relying on a remembered interval.
- 91.417: owner/operator maintenance record retention, including records of alterations. (Paragraph-level verification recommended - see Section 8.)

====================================================================
7. AMT / INSTRUCTIONAL FRAMING (the requester wrote 'FAA-AMT')
====================================================================
For Part 147 / AMT test preparation the defensible three-point statement is:
  1. A&P certificate = perform and supervise maintenance and alteration (65.81), with return-to-service authority for work performed that is not a major repair or major alteration.
  2. Major alteration = needs approved technical data and an approval for return to service by a person authorized under 43.7 - in practice an IA under 65.95(a)(1), or a repair station, or the FAA by field approval.
  3. IA eligibility = A&P held at least 3 years (both ratings), fixed base, actively engaged, equipment/facilities/inspection data, and the IA written test - which is expressly a test on returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations.

====================================================================
8. CITATION VERIFICATION STATUS (so the reader knows what is verbatim vs. summarized)
====================================================================
VERBATIM, from fetched eCFR pages:
  - 65.95(a) privileges text.
  - 65.91 written-test clause.
  - AC 43-210A sentence on approved technical data (attributed quotation; paragraph letters as printed in the AC).
SUBSTANCE-SUMMARIZED - paragraph letters not captured in my source set; confirm at eCFR before quoting in a formal document:
  - 65.91 eligibility subparagraphs (items 1-5).
  - 65.92 (duration) and 65.93 (renewal option list).
  - 43.5(a) conditions; 43.7(c)-(f) categories; 43.9 record content; 91.417 record retention.
  - 65.85 / 65.87 (mechanic 'additional privileges' for airframe and powerplant ratings) - I deliberately do not quote these, because the minor/major return-to-service wording is the exact point on which the mechanic-vs-IA distinction is argued; verify the current text directly.

====================================================================
9. BOTTOM LINE
====================================================================
Inspection Authorization for major alterations = 14 CFR Part 65, Subpart D. Eligibility: 65.91 (A&P with both ratings in effect at least 3 years; fixed base; actively engaged; equipment, facilities and inspection data; IA written test covering return to service after major repairs and major alterations). Privilege: 65.95(a)(1) - inspect and approve for return to service after a major alteration only where the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator, and not on aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program. Supporting rules: 43.5, 43.7(b), 1.1 and Part 43 Appendix A (major alteration classification), Part 21 (STC/design approval route), AC 43-210A and FAA Order 8900.1 (data approval and field-approval boundary), 43.9/91.417 and FAA Form 337 (records).

verdict.summary:
## Short answer

For an FAA aviation maintenance technician (AMT), an inspection authorization (IA) is not a stand-alone certificate. It is an authorization held by a mechanic who already holds a currently effective mechanic certificate with both Airframe and Powerplant ratings. The IA qualification for major alterations has two parts: (1) eligibility and currency to hold the IA, and (2) the scope of the IA privilege to inspect and approve a major alteration for return to service.

The controlling eCFR citations are 14 CFR 65.91(c) (eligibility), 65.92 (duration), 65.93(b) (renewal), 65.95(a)(1) (privilege), and 43.7(b) (return-to-service approval).

In one sentence: an IA may inspect and approve for return to service an aircraft or related part or appliance after a major repair or major alteration, except an aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program, and only if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator.

## 1. Eligibility to obtain an IA — 14 CFR 65.91(c)

An applicant for an inspection authorization must:

1. Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each currently effective and in effect for a total of at least **3 years**.
2. Have been actively engaged, for at least the **2-year period** before the application date, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with 14 CFR.
3. Have a fixed base of operations at which the applicant may be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week; it need not be the place where the IA will be exercised.
4. Have available the equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance.
5. Pass a written test on the applicant’s ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after **major repairs and major alterations** and for annual and progressive inspections performed under Part 43.

If the applicant fails the written test, 14 CFR 65.91(d) prohibits retesting for at least **90 days** after the failure.

Important nuance: initial IA eligibility does **not** require a prior count of major alterations. Major alterations are relevant to the IA privilege and are one of the renewal activity options.

## 2. Duration and renewal — 14 CFR 65.92 and 65.93

- Each inspection authorization expires on **March 31 of each odd-numbered year** (65.92(a)).
- The holder may exercise IA privileges only while both the mechanic certificate and the inspection authorization are currently effective.
- An IA ceases to be effective if the holder surrenders it, is under suspension or revocation, ceases to be actively engaged in maintaining aircraft, fails to have the required equipment/facilities/inspection data, or fails to have the required fixed base (65.92(b)).
- Renewal under 65.93(b) requires meeting 65.91(c)(1) through (4) and, during the **24 months** before the renewal application, at least one of the following:
  1. Performed at least one annual inspection for each **90 days** the authorization was held;
  2. Performed at least **two major repairs or major alterations**;
  3. Performed or supervised and approved at least one progressive inspection;
  4. Attended and completed an acceptable refresher course of not less than **8 hours** of instruction; or
  5. Passed an oral test by an FAA inspector.

Thus, for an IA holder whose recent work is major alterations, the renewal route is **two major repairs or major alterations in the preceding 24 months**, unless another renewal option is used.

## 3. Authority for major alterations — 14 CFR 65.95(a)(1) and 43.7(b)

14 CFR 65.95(a)(1) provides that the holder of an inspection authorization may:

> “Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator.”

14 CFR 43.7(b) provides:

> “The holder of a mechanic certificate or an inspection authorization may approve an aircraft, airframe, aircraft engine, propeller, appliance, or component part for return to service as provided in Part 65 of this chapter.”

Practical meaning for a major alteration:

- The IA privilege is an **inspection and approval** privilege. It is not a license to perform a major alteration without approved technical data.
- The alteration must have been accomplished in accordance with **technical data approved by the FAA Administrator**.
- The IA must actually perform the inspection and make the airworthiness determination. FAA IA guidance states that, with the Part 121 continuous airworthiness exception, an IA may inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance after a major repair or major alteration.
- The exception is an aircraft maintained under a **Part 121 continuous airworthiness program**. The IA does not have this return-to-service authority for those aircraft.
- The major repair or alteration is recorded on **FAA Form 337, Major Repair and Alteration**, as part of the Part 43 records. The IA’s approval is not a substitute for the approved technical data; both the approved data and the IA inspection/approval are required.

## 4. Qualification checklist

| Item | Requirement | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanic certificate | Currently effective mechanic certificate with both Airframe and Powerplant ratings | 65.91(c)(1) |
| Rating currency | Both ratings currently effective and in effect for a total of at least 3 years | 65.91(c)(1) |
| Recent experience | Actively engaged for at least the 2 years before application in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under 14 CFR | 65.91(c)(2) |
| Fixed base | Fixed base of operations where locatable in person or by telephone during a normal working week | 65.91(c)(3) |
| Equipment/facilities/data | Available equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or related parts/appliances | 65.91(c)(4) |
| Written test | Pass the FAA IA written test, including major repairs and major alterations and annual/progressive inspections under Part 43 | 65.91(c)(5) |
| Retest wait | At least 90 days after a failed test before retesting | 65.91(d) |
| Duration | Expires March 31 of each odd-numbered year | 65.92(a) |
| Renewal | Meet 65.91(c)(1)-(4) plus one 24-month activity option, including at least two major repairs or major alterations | 65.93(b) |
| Major-alteration privilege | Inspect and approve for return to service after a major alteration, except Part 121 continuous airworthiness aircraft, if work was done under Administrator-approved technical data | 65.95(a)(1) |
| Return-to-service authority | Mechanic certificate or IA holder may approve for return to service as provided in Part 65 | 43.7(b) |

## 5. What the IA qualification does not mean

- Holding an IA does not authorize a major alteration to be performed without FAA-approved technical data.
- Holding an IA does not override the Part 121 continuous airworthiness program exception.
- Initial IA eligibility does not require a specific number of major alterations; the “two major repairs or major alterations” figure is a renewal activity option under 65.93(b)(2).
- The IA is not limited by aircraft category in the eligibility text of 65.91; the express limitation in the major-alteration privilege is the Part 121 continuous airworthiness exception and the approved-data requirement.

## Sources

- 14 CFR Part 65, current eCFR: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65
- 14 CFR Part 43, current eCFR: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-43
- FAA Inspection Authorization Information Guide: https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/ia_info_guide.pdf
- FAA AC 43-10C: https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC%2043-10C.pdf

verdict.summary:
# Qualifications for Inspection Authorization (IA) Regarding Major Alterations — 14 CFR Part 65 (FAA, U.S.)

## 0. How the question is read

- **"Inspection auth"** = the **Inspection Authorization (IA)** issued under **14 CFR Part 65, Subpart D**. The regulation itself uses the phrase "inspection authorization" and locates its eligibility in **§ 65.91** and its privileges in **§ 65.95**.
- **"(FAA-AMT)"** = the FAA Aviation Maintenance Technician (A&P mechanic certificate, Part 65 Subpart D §§ 65.71–65.89) context.
- **Critical distinction the answer turns on:** an **IA is not a rating on the mechanic certificate**. It is a **separate authorization** layered on top of a mechanic certificate. Holding an A&P does **not** by itself give authority to approve a major alteration for return to service; the IA does.
- **"Regarding major alterations"** is answered on two legs: **(A)** what qualifies a person to *hold* an IA, and **(B)** what conditions attach when that person *uses* the IA on a major alteration.
- Jurisdiction: **United States, 14 CFR** (Title 14, Chapter I, Subchapter D). Not EASA/Transport Canada/ICAO.

---

## 1. Short answer

To inspect and approve a **major alteration** for return to service, a person must hold an **Inspection Authorization** under 14 CFR Part 65 Subpart D, and to be **eligible** for that authorization the applicant must satisfy **all five** elements of **§ 65.91(c)** — most importantly a **currently effective mechanic certificate with BOTH an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each in effect for a total of at least 3 years**, and **at least the 2-year period immediately before application actively engaged in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under 14 CFR**. Having the IA is necessary but not sufficient: when actually approving a major alteration, **§ 65.95(a)(1)** further requires that the **work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator**, that the approval be made **in accordance with Part 43**, and the privilege **does not extend to aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program**.

---

## 2. Leg A — Eligibility to hold the IA: § 65.91(c), five elements (all required)

| # | Requirement (§ 65.91(c)) | What it means in practice | How it is evidenced |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Hold a **currently effective mechanic certificate with both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating**, each currently effective and **in effect for a total of at least 3 years** | You must be an **A&P** — airframe **and** powerplant. An airframe-only or powerplant-only mechanic is **not eligible**. The 3-year clock runs on the ratings being in effect. | Mechanic certificate with both ratings; certificate dates |
| 2 | Have been **actively engaged, for at least the 2-year period before the date of application**, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with 14 CFR | The 2 years must be immediately preceding the application and must be 14 CFR-governed aircraft maintenance work. | Employment/experience record, logbook, employer statements |
| 3 | Have a **fixed base of operations** at which the applicant may be located **in person or by telephone during a normal working week** — it need not be where the inspection authority is exercised | A reachable business location. | Address/phone declared on application |
| 4 | Have **available the equipment, facilities, and inspection data** necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance | Access to current manuals, service data, tooling, and a place to do the inspection. | Applicant's declaration; FAA surveillance |
| 5 | **Pass a written test** on ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service **after major repairs and major alterations** and annual and progressive inspections performed under Part 43 | The IA knowledge test is expressly built around **major repair and major alteration** return-to-service judgment. | IA written test results |

Notes on § 65.91 that must be read in the current eCFR text rather than taken from this summary:

- **§ 65.91(a)–(b):** application form/manner prescribed by the Administrator; an applicant meeting the section is entitled to the authorization.
- **§ 65.91(d):** a **retest waiting period** applies after failing the written test. The exact interval is stated in the regulation — read it there; it is not quoted in this deliverable and no interval is asserted here.

**Direct consequence for an AMT:** the IA is an *additional* step. Minimum path is: mechanic certificate with **both** ratings → **3 years** with both ratings in effect → **2 years** of active 14 CFR maintenance engagement immediately before applying → fixed base, equipment/data, written test.

---

## 3. Leg B — Using the IA on a major alteration: § 65.95(a)(1)

Verbatim (see § 7 for source and retrieval metadata):

> "(1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; and"

Decomposed, the conditions on the major-alteration privilege are:

1. **Holder status** — the person must be the holder of an inspection authorization (§ 65.95(a) opening).
2. **Subject matter** — an aircraft, or related part or appliance, that has undergone a **major repair or major alteration**.
3. **Exclusion** — **not** an aircraft maintained under a **Part 121 continuous airworthiness program**. Those are outside this IA privilege.
4. **Method** — the inspection and approval for return to service must be **in accordance with Part 43** (see § 5 below for the Part 43 hooks).
5. **Technical-data condition** — the alteration must have been **done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator**. An alteration accomplished on unapproved data is not approvable under this paragraph.

§ 65.95(a)(2) is the companion privilege for **annual and progressive inspections**, and § 65.95(b) and following contain limitations on the authorization — read those paragraphs in the current text; they are not paraphrased here.

---

## 4. What an AMT **without** an IA may and may not do on a major alteration

- An A&P **may perform** the work of a major alteration (it is maintenance/alteration within § 43.3 privileges).
- An A&P **may not approve a major alteration for return to service on the strength of the mechanic certificate alone.** Approval for return to service after a major alteration is a distinct act, and the class of persons authorized to do it is set by **§ 43.7** (holders of an inspection authorization, repair stations, and other enumerated persons) subject to **§ 43.5**.
- Therefore, in the AMT context, "inspection authority regarding major alterations" = **the IA privilege in § 65.95(a)(1)**, and the qualifications are the § 65.91(c) eligibility elements plus the § 65.95(a)(1) exercise conditions.

---

## 5. Threshold question — is it a *major* alteration?

Before any of the above applies, the alteration must be classified.

- **14 CFR 1.1 — "Major alteration"**: an alteration **not listed in the aircraft, aircraft engine, or propeller specifications** that **(1)** might appreciably affect weight, balance, structural strength, performance, powerplant operation, flight characteristics, or other qualities affecting airworthiness; **or (2)** is not done according to accepted practices or cannot be done by elementary operations.
- **14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A** carries the enumerated **major alteration** criteria (airframes, aircraft engines, propellers, appliances). Appendix A is where the classification is actually worked out in practice.
- If the alteration is **minor**, the IA major-alteration privilege in § 65.95(a)(1) is not the operative authority.

---

## 6. Part 43 hooks that ride along with an IA major-alteration approval

Read and apply the current text of each; the function of each is stated, not its wording:

| Section | Function in a major alteration |
|---|---|
| **§ 43.5** | Conditions precedent to approval for return to service (record entry made, required repair/alteration form executed, and — where weight/balance or flight characteristics change — test flight where applicable). |
| **§ 43.7** | Persons authorized to approve for return to service; this is the provision that routes major alterations to the IA (among others). |
| **§ 43.9** | Content, form, and disposition of maintenance/alteration record entries. |
| **§ 43.11** | Approval for return to service after annual/progressive inspection (companion IA privilege, § 65.95(a)(2)). |
| **Part 43 Appendix B** | Record of major repair and major alteration — the basis for **FAA Form 337**. |
| **§ 91.409** (and §§ 91.417, 91.419) | Inspection program and record-retention context in which IA approvals live for Part 91 operators. |

---

## 7. Verbatim verified regulatory text

**§ 65.91 (eligibility — the qualification list):**

> "(1) Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each of which is currently effective and has been in effect for a total of at least 3 years;
> (2) Have been actively engaged, for at least the 2-year period before the date he applies, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with this chapter;
> (3) Have a fixed base of operations at which he may be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week but it need not be the place where he will exercise his inspection authority;
> (4) Have available to him the equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance; and
> (5) Pass a written test on his ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations and annual and progressive inspections performed under part 43 of this chapter."
> — http://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D/section-65.91 (fetched 2026-11-13T23:03:33Z, sha256 8dd2b52b76db)

**§ 65.95(a)(1) (the major-alteration privilege):**

> "(1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; and"
> — https://ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D/section-65.95 (fetched 2026-11-13T23:03:33Z, sha256 04eedc455339)

Everything else in this deliverable is either a section pointer (read the text) or a plain-language statement of function.

---

## 8. Currency, duration, and renewal — read these, do not rely on memory

These are the sections a requester must open in the current eCFR because they are amended periodically and **no numeric cycle is asserted in this deliverable**:

- **§ 65.92 — Inspection authorization: duration.** Governs when an IA expires. Read the current expiration rule.
- **§ 65.93 — Inspection authorization: renewal.** Governs the renewal application window and the activity/refresher options that must be shown. Read the current text.
- **§ 65.91(d)** — retest waiting period after a failed written test.
- **§ 65.95(b) and following** — limitations on the authorization.

---

## 9. Source list (eCFR, Title 14, Chapter I, Subchapter D)

Primary (verified in this deliverable):

- https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D

Required to complete the picture (open and read):

- § 65.93 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D/section-65.93

- Part 43: § 43.3, § 43.5, § 43.7, § 43.9, § 43.11, Appendix A, Appendix B — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-43
- § 1.1 (definitions) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-1/section-1.1

Supplemental FAA guidance (not regulation; confirms interpretation):

---

## 10. Procedure to confirm this answer against current law (repeatable)

1. Open `https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D`. Confirm the Subpart D section list still runs 65.91 (inspection authorization), 65.92 (duration), 65.93 (renewal), 65.95 (privileges and limitations).
2. Open **§ 65.91** and confirm the five eligibility elements, specifically the words **"both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating"**, **"at least 3 years"**, and **"at least the 2-year period before the date he applies"**. If any of those three phrases has changed, the qualification answer changes and this deliverable must be reissued.
3. Open **§ 65.95(a)(1)** and confirm the three operative conditions: **major repair or major alteration**, **"in accordance with part 43"**, **"technical data approved by the Administrator"**, and the **Part 121 continuous airworthiness exclusion**.
4. Note the eCFR "current" date and the amendment/FR citation shown at the head of each section; record it as the as-of date of the answer.
5. Open **§§ 65.92 and 65.93** and record the current duration and renewal requirements — these are the two items most likely to be stale if quoted from memory.
6. Open **Part 43 Appendix A** and **§ 1.1** to confirm the major-alteration classification criteria used, and **Part 43 Appendix B** for the Form 337 record requirement.

---

## 11. Limits of this deliverable

- Current-text only. No historical/version comparison is provided; eCFR point-in-time versions would be needed for that.
- No legal advice and no FAA interpretation letters are cited. Where FAA guidance (IA Information Guide, IA ACS, Order 8900.1) is listed, it is guidance, not regulation, and cannot enlarge or contract the § 65.91/§ 65.95 text.
- Sections marked "read the text" (§ 65.91(d), § 65.92, § 65.93, § 65.95(b) and following, and the Part 43 provisions other than those quoted) are cited by function only. No numeric cycle, window, or interval from those sections is asserted here, deliberately, to avoid stating an out-of-date figure.
